summary: Describes the Base45 encoding scheme, which sits alongside Base64, Base32, and Base16 as a way to represent binary data using text characters. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: Computers sometimes need to write secret-looking bytes using only ordinary letters and digits. Base45 is one recipe for that translation, like a code book.

why use base45 for qr codes
subtitle: A compact text encoding for binary data, optimized for QR codes.

tldr.problem: QR codes in Alphanumeric mode can only encode 45 character types, making standard Base64 and Base32 inefficient. Binary data must be converted to text before encoding in a QR code.
tldr.mechanism: Base45 uses those 45 characters to encode 2 bytes in 3 characters (versus Base64's 3-in-4), by treating byte pairs as 16-bit numbers and converting them to base-45 representation.
tldr.outcome: QR codes using Base45 are smaller than those using Base64 or Base32 for the same binary data, saving space when encoding certificates, tickets, and other compact credentials.

today: RFC 9285 is an Internet Standard track informational document published in August 2022 and remains the authoritative specification for Base45 encoding. It is actively used in credential systems that rely on QR codes.

sections.title: Introduction to Base45
sections.content:
Base45 is an encoding scheme that converts binary data into text using 45 specific characters. It is designed for use in QR codes, particularly in the Alphanumeric mode defined by the QR code standard (ISO 18004), which natively supports only 45 characters.

Unlike Base64 and Base32, which are described in RFC 4648, Base45 does not use padding. This makes it more compact when encoding short amounts of binary data. Base45 is particularly useful for encoding credentials such as vaccination certificates (as seen in EU Digital COVID certificates) that need to fit compactly into a QR code.
sections.plainLanguage: Base45 is a recipe to turn bytes (the numbers 0-255) into letters and digits. It fits more data into the same space than older recipes like Base64.

sections.title: How Base45 Encoding Works
sections.content:
Base45 encodes data in pairs of bytes. Two bytes [a, b] are treated as a single 16-bit number: n = (a × 256) + b. This number is then converted to base-45 representation as three digits [c, d, e], where n = c + (d × 45) + (e × 45²). The three digits are then looked up in the Base45 alphabet to produce three characters.

If the input has an odd number of bytes, the last byte is encoded separately as a 8-bit number, converted to base-45 as [c, d], and produces two characters. For example, the byte pair [65, 66] (ASCII 'AB') equals 16706 in base 256, which equals 11 + (11 × 45) + (8 × 45²) in base 45, producing the encoded string 'BB8'.
sections.plainLanguage: Take two bytes, treat them as one big number, then write that number in base-45 using special characters. One byte becomes two characters, two bytes become three characters.

sections.title: The Base45 Alphabet
sections.content:
The Base45 alphabet consists of exactly 45 characters: the digits 0-9, the uppercase letters A-Z, and the special characters space, $, %, *, +, -, ., /, and :. These are the 45 characters permitted in QR code Alphanumeric mode. The order matters: the character at position 0 is '0', position 1 is '1', and so forth up to position 44, which is ':'.

Decoding reverses the process: each character is looked up to find its numeric value, characters are grouped into chunks of three (or two for the final group if odd), and those chunks are converted back to base-45 numbers, which are then converted to byte pairs or single bytes.
sections.plainLanguage: The alphabet is 45 characters: 0-9, A-Z, and a few symbols like $ and :. Each character stands for a number 0 to 44.

sections.title: When to Use Base45
sections.content:
Base45 is best used when binary data must be stored or transmitted in a QR code, particularly in Alphanumeric mode, where its compactness matters. It is not recommended for data being sent over email or HTTP, where Base64 is more standard and better supported. Layering encodings (Base45 on top of Base64) is wasteful and defeats the purpose.

The RFC emphasizes that for any transport other than QR codes, you should choose an encoding suitable for that transport. Base45 solves a specific problem: fitting binary data into the smallest possible QR code.
sections.plainLanguage: Use Base45 when you need to put data in a QR code. Don't use it for email or web pages; use Base64 for those instead.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Implementations must be careful when decoding Base45 to avoid buffer overflows and to handle all byte values (0-255), including the NUL character (ASCII 0). A decoder must validate that input contains only characters from the Base45 alphabet; any character outside the alphabet must be rejected.

Special care is needed with odd-length input and output. A triplet of Base45 characters may decode to a 16-bit value greater than 65535, which is invalid and must be rejected. The RFC provides the example: 'FGW' is valid (equals 65535), but 'GGW' is invalid (would equal 65536, which exceeds 16 bits). Implementations MUST reject such invalid triplets.
sections.plainLanguage: When reading Base45, make sure every character is real, and watch out for triplets that would produce numbers that are too big.
